classification.difficultyReason: Students convert between root and index notation, obtain decimal values, and distinguish rational roots from surds, including recognising that a recurring decimal can be rational. The table and completed example organise these linked decisions.

inlines.text: Complete the table. For irrational values, give decimals to 9 decimal places.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}4^{\frac12}&=\sqrt4\\&=2\end{aligned}$$ The value is rational, so it is not a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{11}&=11^{\frac12}\\\sqrt{11}&\approx3.316624790\end{aligned}$$ The root is irrational, so it is a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{36}&=36^{\frac12}\\\sqrt{36}&=6\end{aligned}$$ The value is rational, so it is not a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac19\right)^{\frac12}&=\sqrt{\frac19}\\&=\frac13\\&=0.\dot3\end{aligned}$$ The value is rational, so it is not a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}(0.1)^{\frac12}&=\sqrt{0.1}\\&\approx0.316227766\end{aligned}$$ The root is irrational, so it is a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}3^{\frac13}&=\sqrt[3]{3}\\&\approx1.442249570\end{aligned}$$ The root is irrational, so it is a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{8}&=8^{\frac13}\\\sqrt[3]{8}&=2\end{aligned}$$ The value is rational, so it is not a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}15^{\frac13}&=\sqrt[3]{15}\\&\approx2.466212074\end{aligned}$$ The root is irrational, so it is a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac1{27}\right)^{\frac13}&=\sqrt[3]{\frac1{27}}\\&=\frac13\\&=0.\dot3\end{aligned}$$ The value is rational, so it is not a surd.
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt[4]{5}&=5^{\frac14}\\\sqrt[4]{5}&\approx1.495348781\end{aligned}$$ The root is irrational, so it is a surd.
